summary: IGNISYNC turns NASA FIRMS satellite data into a fire activity calendar for southeast Australia. It counts each grid cell once per day when it contains a qualifying detection, then converts VIIRS measurements to the Aqua MODIS scale. In testing, this reduced the average monthly difference from Aqua by about 84%.
details:
When two satellites observe the same place and report different levels of activity, how can a land manager compare that place’s burning history over time? IGNISYNC is a web prototype that addresses this problem using NASA’s Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS). Our case study covers a region in southeast Australia and uses 1,561,056 historical detection records from 48 FIRMS files prepared for the study area.

The project is designed around a practical question. A researcher selects an area and a date range, opens a month such as December 2019, and compares its observed activity with the same month in other years. A monthly calendar provides the historical view, and the map shows where the underlying detections were recorded. The prototype currently lets users inspect verified source records by month and trace them to their original files.

To make the two records comparable, we calculate a monthly indicator called active cell-days. We filter observations to the study area and apply the confidence criteria for each instrument. On a shared, equal-area grid of 10 km cells, we count each cell once per UTC day if it contains at least one eligible detection. This gives both instruments a common unit and reduces the effect of multiple detections in the same cell on the same day.

We use Aqua MODIS as the historical reference and estimate a conversion from S-NPP VIIRS using months when both instruments observed the region. In our regional data experiment, we fitted the conversion on 72 months from 2013 through 2018 and evaluated it on a separate 48-month period from 2021 through 2024. The mean absolute monthly difference from Aqua fell from 377.46 to 61.32 active cell-days, an 83.8% reduction compared with the unconverted VIIRS indicator. A seasonal median baseline produced a difference of 87.92. The model still underestimated the December 2019 peak, which highlights the need to examine individual high-activity months alongside average performance.

The proposed calendar combines observed Aqua values with eligible VIIRS estimates on the Aqua reference scale. It identifies the source of each value and distinguishes missing data from months with zero eligible detections. When the conversion is ineligible, users can review the two sensor records separately. The experiment measures agreement with Aqua within the study area. Assessing accuracy on the ground would require independent observations.

We built the interface with Next.js and TypeScript, the backend with Python and FastAPI, and the local data pipeline with DuckDB and Parquet. OpenCode assisted with software development.
